opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more underappreciated connections right now. A lot of what reinforcement learning does in the current post-training setups is really sharpening what's already in the base model. When you look carefully, RL with verifiable rewards often isn't teaching the model fundamentally new reasoning abilities so much as it's reweighting the distribution, pushing probability mass toward good trajectories the base model could already produce, just not reliably.

So if that's the picture, then how well you can sample from the base model matters a lot. RL can only reinforce what it actually sees. If your sampling is narrow, if you keep drawing the same high-likelihood but mediocre completions, you never surface the rare good trajectories, and you get very little useful signal, especially on hard problems where the reward is sparse. Better sampling, whether that's smarter decoding, sampling that targets a sharper version of the base distribution, or methods that encourage diversity, effectively gives RL a better starting set of candidates to learn from.

There's also an interesting flip side. Some recent work suggests that if you sample from the base model more cleverly, say by approximating a power or sharpened distribution, you can recover a surprising amount of the gains people attribute to RL without any training at all. To me that's not a threat to RL. It's a diagnostic. It tells us which part of the improvement is just about extracting latent capability, and which part genuinely requires learning. And it suggests a division of labor: use good sampling to do the cheap extraction, then focus RL compute on the parts where the model really needs to move beyond its prior.

The other piece I care about is diversity and robustness. RL tends to collapse the output distribution. You get higher pass-at-one, but pass-at-k across many samples can actually go down, because you've lost coverage. If you start from better, more diverse sampling and keep that in mind as part of training, you can avoid over-committing too early and end up with models that are both more accurate and less brittle when they face something slightly outside what they were trained on.

So I'd say improved base-model sampling contributes in three ways: better exploration and denser signal during RL, a clearer understanding of what RL is actually adding, and a way to preserve diversity so we don't trade generalization for short-term benchmark gains.

r001.rationale: The response says better base-model sampling gives RL better candidates and improves exploration and training signal.

r002.rationale: It links diversity to better exploration and coverage, but does not clearly state that controlling sample diversity enables structured exploration across different spaces.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it gets at the question of where the capability in RL actually comes from. The way RL fine-tuning works, especially with outcome-based rewards, is that you sample from the model, you check which samples get the answer right, and you reinforce those. So the whole process is fundamentally bottlenecked by what the base model can produce in the first place. If the correct solution never shows up in your samples, there's nothing to reinforce. You can't learn from a reward signal you never see.

So the way I think about it is that the base model's sampling distribution defines the search space, and RL is essentially sharpening that distribution toward the regions that get reward. There's been a bunch of work, including some from my group, looking at pass-at-k as a kind of diagnostic for this. If you look at a base model and ask, does the right answer appear anywhere in, say, a thousand samples, you often find that it does, even on problems where the single-sample accuracy is very low. And what RL does is move that probability mass so the answer shows up in one sample instead of one in a thousand.

Which means that improvements in base-model sampling, whether that's better pretraining, better diversity in the outputs, or just a model that covers a broader space of reasonable solution attempts, translate pretty directly into what RL can get you. If the base model has broader coverage, RL has more to work with. And conversely, one of the failure modes we've seen is that RL can actually collapse diversity. You sharpen toward the solutions that work on the training distribution, and you lose some of the exploration that would have helped you on harder or out-of-distribution problems. So there's this tension where you want to exploit what the base model already knows, but you also don't want to prematurely narrow the distribution.

The thing I find interesting is that this reframes a lot of the debate about whether RL teaches models genuinely new capabilities or just surfaces latent ones. I think the honest answer is mostly the latter right now, but that's not a knock on RL. It's just telling you that the leverage is in making sure the base model has the right things in its distribution to begin with, and then designing the RL procedure so it doesn't throw away the diversity it needs for the next round of improvement.

r001.rationale: The response says improvements in base-model sampling translate directly into what RL can achieve and give RL more to work with.

r002.rationale: It discusses broader coverage, diversity, and preserving exploration, but does not state that greater control over sample diversity enables structured exploration across different spaces.

astra-6.text:
I think better base models make reinforcement learning much more effective because they change what you can discover through sampling. If the base model already has some probability of producing a good solution, then you can sample several attempts, identify which ones work, and use reinforcement learning to make those successful behaviors more likely.

The difficult case is when the model almost never produces a successful solution. Then you don’t get much useful signal from a reward that only tells you whether the final answer is correct. So improvements in the base model can make problems accessible to RL that previously weren’t, simply because successful trajectories start appearing in your samples.

But I’d distinguish being able to find a good answer after many samples from reliably producing one in a single attempt. Reinforcement learning can help bridge that gap. And that makes the interaction interesting: better sampling gives you better training experience, and training can turn that experience into a more reliable model.

r001.rationale: The response says better base-model sampling produces useful successful trajectories and training experience, making reinforcement-learning training more effective.

r002.rationale: It describes sampling several attempts, but does not state that greater control over sample diversity enables structured exploration across different spaces.

sol-6.1.text:
I think better sampling from the base model can make reinforcement learning much more effective, because the samples are what you learn from. If the model generates a correct solution occasionally, then you have a signal that lets you reinforce that behavior. But if it never generates anything useful, it’s much harder to make progress, especially with a sparse reward.

So there’s an interesting balance: you want samples that are good enough to provide a learning signal, but you also want enough diversity to explore different solutions. Improving that balance can help you get more out of the same rollout budget. The question I’d want to understand is whether you’re just finding the good solutions more efficiently, or whether that translates into a model that can reliably produce them after training.

r001.rationale: It says better base-model sampling makes reinforcement-learning training more effective by providing useful samples and learning signals.

r002.rationale: It says sample diversity helps explore different solutions, but does not state that greater control over diversity enables structured exploration across different spaces.
